b.bio: The library prints the name as 'Ildefonsus of Seville', but the sources identify this author as Ildefonsus (Ildephonsus) of Toledo — do not confuse him with Isidore of Seville, whose De viris illustribus he continued. Born probably in Toledo around 610 to a distinguished family, nephew of his predecessor St. Eugenius, he entered the monastery of Agali near Toledo against his father's wishes, became its abbot, signed the Eighth and Ninth Councils of Toledo in 653 and 655, and was made Archbishop of Toledo by King Reccesvinth at the end of 657. He governed the see for a little over nine years and died on 23 January 667.
b.s: A leading theologian of Visigothic Spain; the work held here is a short expository piece treating the Trinity, the sacraments, the Eucharist as prefiguring eternal life, and the angelic orders, arguing against apocryphal writings and citing Ezekiel, Athanasius, Sedulius, and Paul.

b.bio: Idatius (Hydatius) was born around 400 at Lemica/Limica (near modern Xinzo de Limia, Galicia); some authorities place his birth as early as c. 388. As a child he travelled with his mother on pilgrimage to Palestine and saw Jerome at Bethlehem. He entered the clergy about 417 and was probably consecrated bishop of Aquae Flaviae (Chaves, Portugal) in 427. He served until shortly after 468, exercising political as well as ecclesiastical influence: in 431 he joined a delegation to Aëtius seeking imperial help against the Suevi, who had settled in Gallaecia in 411. His Chronicle continues Jerome's from 379 to 468, drawing on others' testimony for the earlier years and his own eyewitness for events after 427.
b.s: His Chronicle is the principal evidence for fifth-century Hispania. The works held here include material recording councils condemning Priscillianism by subscription and refuting Nestorius's heresy (with Cyril's letter stating the rule of faith), Augustine defeating the Donatists by God's help, and Jerome refuting Pelagius and his heresy.

b.bio: The library prints this name as 'Idatius of Barcelona', but the surviving records describe a different man: Hydatius (Idatius) of Lemica, bishop of Aquae Flaviae in Gallaecia from about 427, author of a chronicle continuing Jerome. That chronicler cannot be the author of the two pages held here, which cite Julian, bishop of Toledo (died 690), and speak of a compiler gathering orthodox doctrine from the ancient fathers. The letters under this name therefore belong to a later figure, apparently connected with Barcelona and with Julian of Toledo's circle, for whom these sources give no dates or biography.
b.s: The work held here is a citation-survey on last things, resurrection, eternal life, the Church, the Trinity, and grace, presenting itself as prescience of the future age and crediting the patristic material while claiming praise for the compiler's labor.

b.bio: Irmina (also Ermina, Hirmina) was a Frankish noblewoman who founded and ruled as abbess the convent at Oeren (ad Horreum) near Trier, and gave Willibrord land for his monastery at Echternach. Her twelfth-century biography by Thiofrid of Echternach is considered unreliable, and her parentage is disputed: she is variously said to be daughter of Dagobert I or Dagobert II. Ian Wood judges her traditionally, and probably correctly, identified as Plectrude's mother.
b.s: The library holds only a three-page appendix in PL 87 under her name; she matters chiefly as a founder-benefactress of Merovingian monasticism rather than as an author.

b.bio: Isaac of Langres, surnamed 'le Débonnaire' or 'bonus', was bishop of Langres, elected in 857 according to the BnF record (the Cyclopedia says ordained about 856), until his death in 880. Sources differ on his birth: the BnF record gives a date no earlier than 801, while other authorities say c. 820. He had been a deacon of Laon (present at the Council of Kiersy in 840 as such); after Wulfade was compelled to flee the see of Langres, Hilduin, lay abbot of Saint-Denis, proposed Isaac and secured his appointment. He appears in the councils of Toul and Langres (859), Tousy (860), Pistes (862), Verberie and Soissons (866). His Capitula, compiled between 857 and 880, is a collection of 151 canons, chiefly penitential, built on the collection attributed to Benedictus Levita.
b.s: The work held here is his canonical collection on church discipline — penance, clerical immunity from secular service and courts, and the limits of secular jurisdiction over the church — a witness to Carolingian reform legislation.

b.bio: The library prints this author as Isaia Syriae and holds under his name a short ascetic text in PL 103 on sin, prayer, humility, and confession. This is Abba Isaiah of Scetis (also Isaiah of Gaza), an Egyptian monastic writer whom the Deutsche Biographie authority file dates to 0488 and lists under names including 'Isaias, Monophysita', 'Isaias, Moine Egyptien', 'Isaias, von Sketis' and 'Isaias, von Gaza'. He is not Isaac of Nineveh (c. 613–c. 700), the East Syrian bishop: the Catholic Encyclopedia, Wikipedia, and Britannica entries among the sources concern that homonym, a different man of a different century and church, and nothing from those entries applies here.
b.s: The work held here is a brief Latin witness to Egyptian desert teaching on humility, penance, and unceasing prayer, transmitted through the monastic tradition to Western readers.

b.bio: Isidore of Beja (Isidorus Pacensis) was a Lusitanian Catholic priest and bishop of Beja who wrote at the start of the eighth century. He has been confused with the so-called Anonyme de Cordoue, author of a metrical chronicle of the last kings of Toledo; that is a different work and a different author. The chronicle printed under his name in PL 96 is valued because it preserves a contemporary Christian account of the Muslim conquest of the Iberian peninsula.
b.s: His Chronicle is one of the few contemporary Christian narratives of the Arab conquest of Spain, recording figures such as Abdalla's conquest of Africa, the defeat of Constans by Moabia at sea, and civil war dividing the Arab army between two princes.

w: On the Miracles of St. Othmar

b.bio: Iso was born around 830 in Thurgau, near Weinfelden on the right bank of the Thur river, to prosperous parents who dedicated him to monastic life before his birth. He appears in documents as a monk of St. Gallen from 852 and was head of its outer school, the first significant teacher of that school to be individually identifiable; Notker Balbulus and Tutilo were among his pupils before Marcellus took them over with the inner school. He died on 14 May 871 at Münster-Granfelden, where he had become schoolmaster.
b.s: His De miraculis S. Othmari records the miracles at St. Othmar's tomb and argues that prayer there heals the sick, that such miracles manifest the saint's holiness for the faithful's edification, and that relic translation belongs to episcopal authority rather than private initiative.

b.t: Roman Catholic (Clerics Regular of the Mother of God)
b.bio: Ippolito Marracci was born in 1604 and entered the Order of the Clerics Regular of the Mother of God, founded by Giovanni Leonardi at Lucca, in 1621. He spent his career compiling and editing Mariological literature: the Bibliotheca Mariana (1648), Pontifices maximi Mariani (1642), Reges Mariani (1654), Antistites Mariani (1656), and Heroides Marianæ (1659). His brother Ludovico collaborated with him by translating Greek patristic texts on Mary into Latin. He died at Rome on 19 May 1675 in the house of Santa Maria in Campitelli. The works held here are his notes on Adam of Perseigne's Mariale and Marian fragments, edited from a parchment manuscript of Casamari and printed in 1652.
b.s: The works here are Marracci's scholarly annotations to the Mariale and Marian fragments of Adam of Perseigne, which he recovered from an old manuscript and supplied with notes citing Bonaventure, Antoninus, Albert the Great, Richard of St. Lawrence, Augustine, Peter Damian, Ephrem, and Ildephonsus.

b.bio: Ildefons von Arx, born Urs Joseph Nicolaus von Arx at Olten on 3 October 1755, entered the Benedictine abbey of St. Gallen as a novice in 1773 and took the name Ildefons at his profession in 1774; he was ordained priest in 1781. After conflicts with Prince-Abbot Beda Angehrn over the abbey's finances he was transferred to Hemberg (1788) and Ebringen in the Breisgau (1789), where he wrote a history of that lordship. Recalled by Abbot Pankraz Vorster in 1796, he served on the St. Gallen interim government in 1797 and organized the Olten and St. Gallen archives while writing several histories, including his three-volume Geschichten des Kantons St. Gallen (1810–1813). When the abbey was dissolved in 1805 he worked under archivist Konrad Meyer, and from 1823 until his death at St. Gallen on 16 October 1833 he was librarian of the Stiftsbibliothek.
b.s: The single page held here is a historical notice printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 126, where von Arx appears as a modern scholarly contributor rather than an ancient author; readers should treat him as the 19th-century Benedictine archivist and historian of St. Gallen, not a patristic writer.

b.bio: An Egyptian monk of the desert of Scete, active around the turn of the fifth century, known chiefly through sayings in the Apophthegmata patrum and through an Asceticon collected after his death by his disciple Peter. His identity is disputed: the older identification with Isaiah of Gaza (d. ca. 488), a Miaphysite figure described by Zacharias the Scholastic, was refuted by Draguet in 1968, so the author of the Asceticon remains a distinct, uncertain figure. The work held here is the Greek ascetical corpus printed in Migne's Patrologia Graeca 40.
b.s: The Asceticon was influential in the development of Eastern Christian asceticism and spirituality, treating sin, watchfulness of the heart, prayer, and the virtues for monks and solitaries.

b.bio: Isaac II Angelos was Byzantine emperor from September 1185, when the Constantinople mob that had murdered his cousin Andronikos I Komnenos proclaimed him emperor, until his deposition by his brother Alexios III in April 1195; he was restored as co-emperor with his son Alexios IV in July 1203 and died in Constantinople in late January/February 1204. Sources disagree on his birth year: Wikipedia and the Oxford Dictionary of Byzantium give September/ca. 1156, Britannica c. 1135, so a wider range is printed here. His reign was inaugurated by his general Alexius Branas's victory over the Normans who had invaded and sacked Thessalonica in 1185, and he partly retrieved imperial fortunes in the Balkans by defeating the Serbians in 1190, though he was incapable of stemming administrative abuses. The library holds one short historical text under his name from PG 135.
b.s: The single work held here is a brief historical account of an episcopal election dispute, arguing that elections require all resident bishops present or consulted, that canons reject elections lacking synodal consent, that the emperor holds authority to correct church abuses, and that episcopal ordination requires prior marital separation by mutual consent — directed against the metropolitan and bishop of Cyzicus and citing Emperor Manuel Comnenus.

b.bio: Isidore was born at Thessalonica towards the end of the fourteenth century; his nationality is uncertain (Greek or Bulgar), but his education was wholly Greek. A monk and hegumenos of St Demetrius at Constantinople, he was sent by Emperor John VIII to Basle in 1434 and chosen by Patriarch Joseph II as metropolitan of Kiev in 1437. A committed supporter of union with Rome, he attended the Council of Ferrara–Florence, proclaimed the union at Hagia Sophia on 12 December 1452, and after Constantinople fell returned to Rome, where he held the cardinalate of Sabina and the Latin patriarchate of Constantinople. He died in Rome on 27 April 1463.
b.s: The work held here is a Greek homiletic text on the Virgin Mary, arguing from fittingness that all things existed for her sake, that God became incarnate because no creature sufficed for man's restoration, and that her shared nature makes her a model of holiness.
